flawed_step: Lines 0031-0046 (case management of the exponent 0): line 0031 opens the case 'either p = 0 or q = 0' but lines 0033-0038 only restate the definition M_0 = G and never prove any inequality; line 0040 then declares 'It remains to resolve the inequality for p, q in R_{>=0}', explicitly claiming p = 0 is inside the branch that follows, and lines 0042-0046 build that branch on phi(x) = x^{q/p} with derivative (q/p) x^{q/p - 1}, which is undefined when p = 0.
counterexample: Take n = 2, p = 0, q = 1, x_1 = 1, x_2 = 4 (legitimate data for the theorem: p = 0 < q = 1, all x_k >= 0). The claim to be proved is M_0(1,4) = sqrt(1*4) = 2 <= M_1(1,4) = (1+4)/2 = 2.5. Trace the proof on this instance: the infinite-exponent lemmas (0005-0029) say nothing, since neither exponent is +/-infinity. Lines 0033-0038 only assert M_0(1,4) = G(1,4) = 2, with no comparison to anything. Line 0040 then routes this instance (p = 0, q = 1, both in R_{>=0}) into the Jensen branch, where line 0043 requires phi(x) = x^{q/p} = x^{1/0} and line 0046 requires the constant q/p = 1/0 -- both undefined, so lines 0048-0061 produce no inequality at all for this instance. Hence for p = 0, q = 1, x = (1,4) the proof yields no bound whatsoever: the genuinely nontrivial AM-GM instance 2 <= 2.5 is asserted-by-routing but never derived. The same failure occurs for every p = 0 pair, and symmetrically the same defect blocks q = 0 (e.g. p = -1, q = 0, x = (1,4): phi(x) = x^{0/(-1)} = 1 is constant, so Jensen gives only the vacuous equality 1 <= 1 and never M_{-1} = 1.6 <= M_0 = 2). Secondary, independent defect: line 0061 asserts that equality holds iff x_1 = ... = x_n, which contradicts the second disjunct of the theorem's equality clause (q < 0 with some x_k = 0); e.g. n = 2, p = -infinity, q = -1, x = (0,1) gives M_{-infinity} = min = 0 and M_{-1} = 0 (harmonic mean with a zero entry), equality with x_1 != x_2, and the proof's infinite-exponent lemmas (0011-0028) never analyse equality at all.
reasoning_summary: I first attacked the mathematical core (lines 0042-0059) numerically, since the convexity claim is stated in terms of the sign of q alone rather than the exponent q/p. It survives: under the hypothesis p < q with p, q real and nonzero, 0 < p < q gives q/p > 1 (convex), p < 0 < q gives q/p < 0 (convex on (0,inf)), and p < q < 0 gives q/p in (0,1) (concave), so lines 0049 and 0052 are correct in every in-scope case, and spot checks confirm the Jensen directions (p = -1, q = 1, x = (1,2): 0.75^{-1} = 1.333 <= 1.5; p = -2, q = -1, x = (1,2): 0.625^{0.5} = 0.791 >= 0.75, and raising to 1/q < 0 correctly yields M_{-2} = 1.265 <= M_{-1} = 1.333). The refutation instead lands on the case management: the exponent-0 case is announced at line 0031, disposed of with a bare definition, and then explicitly folded back into the Jensen branch by line 0040, whose machinery divides by p. The instance p = 0, q = 1, x = (1,4) walks through the whole proof and emerges with no inequality derived, so the stated theorem (which covers p, q in the extended reals, including 0) is not proved. A second, separate failure is the equality characterisation: line 0061 states an iff that omits the theorem's own second disjunct and is never established for the infinite-exponent branches.
notes: Reported under the counterexample-first protocol; stopped auditing once the p = 0 routing failure was confirmed by tracing an explicit instance.
